HomeBite

Final project report · Nicole Lin · MGT 409, AI Foundations for Managers, Yale SOM, Fall 2026

1. Title and links

Adapt a dish from home to the ingredients you can actually buy at your store, with nutrition computed in code from USDA data.

AuthorNicole Lin
CourseMGT 409, AI Foundations for Managers, Yale SOM, Fall 2026
Repositoryhttps://github.com/kl2278/homebite
AppNot hosted online. Runs locally from a fresh clone; setup measured at about 35 seconds in a fresh-clone test (see README). The README itself estimates about 5 minutes for a first-time user, because that includes creating the .env file.

HomeBite takes a dish that a student misses from home, for example Taiwanese beef noodle soup, together with the student's store and allergies. It breaks the dish into ingredients, finds substitutes for the ones that are hard to buy, but only from a product catalog for that store, writes the cooking steps, and compares the nutrition of the original and the adapted dish. Code, not the AI model, computes the nutrition numbers and checks allergens and vegetarian, vegan and pescatarian diets. It is a prototype: the catalog is a starter set of 163 illustrative items, not real store data.

At a glance
  • Design: four AI agents (Intake, Analyst, Substitution, Writer) and a Verifier that is plain code, plus an input guard (rules and one classifier call) and an output check (code). Model: gpt-6-luna through Portkey.
  • Data: 3,000 USDA foods and 163 catalog items; 0 of the 163 catalog items have been verified against real store listings.
  • Cost and speed (20 live runs, 10 dishes x 2 configurations): baseline average $0.002414 per run and 33.2 seconds per run.
  • Checks: 268 automated tests pass without spending tokens; the safety demo, re-run after the diet fix (it has no diet case), passes 19/19 cases.
  • Honest result: a cheaper configuration cut cost by 16.9% but lowered the nutrition match rate from 91.7% to 82.0%, so I did not adopt it.

2. Motivation: who this is for

The problem

U.S. institutions hosted 1,177,766 international students in 2024/25, about 6% of total U.S. higher-education enrollment (Open Doors 2025). Many of them arrive in a food environment that is unfamiliar. A 2015 study with seven focus groups and 32 college-age international students at an urban U.S. university found that students described many dietary challenges when adapting to American culture, shaped by the food environment, the campus, religion and personal preferences. The authors also report dietary changes associated with undesirable health outcomes such as weight gain (Alakaam et al., 2015).

Where students shop matters. A master's thesis at East Carolina University (142 international students surveyed in spring 2011, plus interviews) found that food choices followed whether native foods were available in local stores; newcomers looked for familiar foods. In a small thesis study at one large public university (38 surveys, 11 interviews), 80% of the students who rated belonging differently for home-country foods versus overall reported more belonging with those foods: a hint, not a measurement.

Money matters too. A survey of 853 students aged 18 to 34 at one Midwest university (April 2022) found food insecurity among 26.8% of international students, against 19.9% of White students and 35.6% of U.S.-born multicultural students. One university only, so this shows the problem exists, not how large it is.

My own starting point

I am an international student from Taiwan. I love cooking and I'm passionate about nutrition. I find it challenging to get used to the food here in the US, and I miss my mom's cooking (or Taiwanese food in general) a lot. I designed this app because I think a lot of international students might share my experience and want to recreate some dishes from home.

How students cope today, and what it costs

The usual workarounds are a web search, asking a chatbot, asking family, or giving up on the dish. I timed one: searching Google for a vegetarian kimchi jjigae recipe took about 2 minutes (one dish, one attempt, self-timed) and produced a recipe only; I still had to look up nutrition facts myself. I did not measure what students spend in money or how often they give up, so I make no claim about either.

What HomeBite is not. It is not medical advice. It does not fix food insecurity. It is not a substitute for real store data: its catalog is a starter set of 163 illustrative items, and none of them has been checked against a real store listing.

3. What is new here, and what is not

I compared HomeBite with three existing products as publicly described, and ran one hands-on test against a general chatbot. Product descriptions come from public announcements and web pages (listed under Sources), as publicly described (2023 launch announcements; features may have changed by October 2026; not hands-on tested by me). The right-hand column says where the other tool is stronger.

ToolWhat it does well (as publicly described)What HomeBite adds or does differentlyWhere it is stronger than HomeBite

Personalize Recipe adapts a saved recipe to dietary requirements; Food AI can swap ingredients; recipes become shopping lists; nutrition is shown.Starts from a specific dish from home and rebuilds it for one named store; every substitute must be a catalog product; a code check re-runs the substitution on an allergen or diet conflict.A full platform with saved recipes and shopping lists.

Is this just another recipe or meal-planning app?

It is adjacent to that crowded category, and the difference is narrow. It starts from one dish from home and rebuilds it for the student's own store; it does not plan meals. The model proposes and code disposes: products can only come from the catalog, nutrition is computed in code from USDA data (ingredients without an entry are listed as excluded), and allergen and vegetarian, vegan or pescatarian conflicts are checked by code and trigger a re-run. "No substitute, leave it out" is an allowed answer, and it happens often (section 8). Safety and cost behavior is measured (20 live runs and a rerunnable safety demo). It is a prototype of a verification layer, not a finished product.

A head-to-head test with a general chatbot

This is one dish, one chatbot, one prompt and one run each. I gave ChatGPT (GPT-6) this request: “I'm an international student shopping at Walmart in the US. Adapt a vegetarian Korean kimchi jjigae using ingredients I can buy there, list the products to buy, and give calories and sodium per serving.” The app displayed “Worked for 1m 15s”. I ran HomeBite on the same dish with Walmart, dietary preference vegetarian, goal lower sodium (the chatbot prompt did not mention a sodium goal), 2 servings and the text “Korean kimchi jjigae”. I ran HomeBite twice more after fixing the problem this test exposed (below): once with the goal set to none, and once with the exact original settings (logged in logs/diet_fix_check.md).

The two nutrition sets are not comparable, because the recipes differ (pork belly or none, and different kimchi products and amounts).

What the test shows. ChatGPT's answer met the vegetarian requirement, named three Walmart products with prices (two of the links I clicked were correct and real), and included photos and an interactive estimate. Its displayed run time was 1 m 15 s against HomeBite's 33 s, but the two did different work, so I do not read the times as an advantage either way. HomeBite's answer at the time of the test was not vegetarian. Two of Alex's three suggestions (section 7), pictures and conversation, are things ChatGPT did here. ChatGPT also named a specific vegan-labeled kimchi, while HomeBite kept generic kimchi with a check-the-label warning because its catalog has no such product.

What HomeBite's checks add, and what this test showed. Catalog-only products: not shown as a benefit; no product was named at all, because the starter catalog had nothing suitable. USDA values computed in code with excluded items listed: shown, but because the recipes differ I cannot say whose numbers are closer to the truth. Allergen and diet checks: the allergen check was not exercised (no allergies selected); the diet check did not exist at the time, and after the fix it flagged pork belly on the first pass and removed it through the re-run (section 6).

4. The agents

HomeBite is a pipeline of small steps. Intake, Analyst, Substitution and Writer are AI agents with a narrow job; the Verifier is plain code; and two more checks sit around them: an input guard (free rules plus one classifier call) and an output check (code). Each agent returns a structured result; the Writer's text is checked before it is shown.

StageJobToolsHands to the next stage
Input guard (rules + 1 AI call)Free rules first (overrides, requests for the prompt or keys, attempts to change store or allergies), then one cheap classifier call; if it cannot run, the request stops.Rules; one AI callPass, or a friendly message with no further tokens
Intake (AI)Turns the text and sidebar settings into a request, or asks one clarifying question.NoneA structured request
Analyst (AI)Breaks the dish into ingredients with weights, flags those hard to find in a U.S. supermarket, finds USDA entries.USDA searchIngredients with USDA ids
Substitution (AI)For each hard-to-find ingredient, picks a product that really comes back from a search of the student's store, or says there is none.Catalog search (store and allergies fixed by code), USDA searchA substitution plan
Verifier (code, no AI)Checks each substitute exists, computes nutrition for both versions, runs the allergen check and the diet check (vegetarian, vegan, pescatarian), lists unmatched ingredients; re-runs Substitution once on a definite conflict.Catalog lookup, nutrition math, checksVerified lists, nutrition, check results
Writer (AI)Writes the intro, steps and a taste note. It never sees nutrition numbers.NoneText
Output check (code)Rejects leaked prompts, key-like strings, invented numbers, nutrition claims and unconfirmed product names; retries once, then uses a plain template.RulesThe text shown, or the template

Which model, and why

All AI calls use gpt-6-luna through Portkey with the course key. I chose the low-cost tier: $0.10 per million input tokens, $0.01 per million cached input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens (course pricing slide), with cache writes at $0.125. The code calls the model through the Responses API, because the chat completions endpoint rejected function tools for this model (a comment in llm.py records this).

Why separate stages instead of one prompt

Separation of duties: the model reads a dish and proposes ingredients, and code computes numbers and checks. Each stage also gets its own small prompt and limits. I did not build or test a single-prompt version, so I cannot report how it would compare in cost or quality.

One real run, step by step

This is a live run of Kung pao chicken with Walmart selected and a peanut allergy (its result page is Figure 9 in section 6). Settings go in the sidebar; the text box holds only the dish name.

Behind the page is a trace of every stage. The panels below are from the same run. The Intake panel shows the trusted settings and the student text in separate delimited blocks. The Analyst ran 21 nutrition searches (counted from the panel) in 3 requests. The Substitution agent searched the catalog five times and found a product for two of them. The Verifier, which is code, confirmed both products exist in the Walmart catalog, computed nutrition twice (original and adapted) and found one allergen conflict, which sent the run back to Substitution once.

Cross-check: the Intake, Analyst, Substitution and Writer panels add up to 11,185 input and 2,981 output tokens; the usage panel reports 13,661 input (2,855 cached) and 3,879 output tokens over 10 requests. The remaining 2,476 input and 898 output tokens are consistent with the guard call and the substitution re-run, whose panels are not shown.

Design choices that are in the code. Store, allergies, diet, servings and goal come from the sidebar as configuration; the student's text is wrapped in delimiters and treated as data. The Analyst is not told the student's allergies: it describes the traditional dish, so a conflicting ingredient reaches the code check instead of being silently dropped by the model.

5. Tokenomics

All numbers in this section come from 20 live runs: 10 dishes, each run once with the baseline configuration and once with a cost-saver configuration (section below). Costs are computed from token counts with the course prices; the guard stage is included in every total. Latency is wall-clock time. No run was flagged as a possible gateway cache hit.

Baseline cost per run

Per run (10 dishes)Averagep90
Input tokens11,70915,291
Cached input tokens3,2656,462
Output tokens2,8294,180
Cost$0.002414$0.003646
Latency (seconds)33.245.1

Cached input is 27.9% of input. Latency ranged from 16.1 to 56.6 seconds across all 20 runs. Cache-write tokens (79,169 across all runs) are priced at the cache-write rate.

Where the cost goes

The guard stage costs $0.000052 per request on average (337 input and 38 output tokens), 2.2% of the total; two real classifier calls in the safety demo used 403 and 401 tokens. Output is priced at five times normal input and is 58.6% of baseline cost.

Cost per user and at scale

The monthly figures use 12 runs per user per month, which is my assumption, not something I measured. They include the guard cost.

1 user: 12 runs, $0.03; 100 users: 1,200 runs, $2.90; 10,000 users: 120,000 runs, $289.72 per month.

They exclude hosting, storage and bandwidth, and they do not model provider rate limits at 100 or 10,000 users. They are estimates from tokens and the course price slide, not an invoice. The per-day token cap of 3,000,000 tokens implies at most about $0.50 per day at the measured token mix ($1.50 in the worst case). The whole 20-run measurement used 242,278 input plus output tokens, about $0.044.

Can the cost be cut?

I tested three levers, switchable by a settings object and off by default: put each agent's static instructions first and the dynamic text last (so provider prompt caching could apply), trim the Analyst and Writer prompts while keeping every safety rule, and add a batched nutrition lookup so the Analyst searches all ingredients in one call. The cost-saver configuration turns on all three together. Each dish was run once per configuration, alternating which went first.

MetricBaselineCost-saverChange
Input tokens11,7097,146-39.0%
Cached input tokens3,265619-81.0%
Output tokens2,8292,545-10.0%
Cost per run$0.002414$0.002006-16.9%
Tool calls19.44.8-75.3%
Latency (s)33.231.7-4.5%
Nutrition match rate (avg)91.7%82.0%
Writer fallback rate0%0%
Catalog valid rate (proposed substitutes found in catalog)100%100%
Allergen detection rate (conflict_detected / expected, 5 dishes)100%100%
Residual allergen conflicts (count)00

Tool calls fell by 75.3% and cost fell by 16.9%; the cost-saver was cheaper on 9 of 10 dishes. The combined cost-saver did not raise caching: cached input fell by 81.0%, so the savings came from fewer tokens, not from more cache hits. Because the three levers were tested together, I cannot say whether prompt order alone had any effect.

The cost-saver was not adopted. It cut cost, but the nutrition match rate fell from 91.7% to 82.0%, and it was lower on 7 of 10 dishes (equal on 3, higher on none), so this is unlikely to be noise alone. A lower match rate means more ingredients are left out of the nutrition totals. I tested the three levers together, so I cannot say which one caused the drop. With one run per dish, the sample is small. The app still runs the baseline configuration.

Defenses working

The classifier calls for the two declined requests used 342 input and 41 output tokens (medical) and 341 input and 67 output tokens (extreme restriction), one request each, as the usage tables show. The safety demo (19/19 cases) covers the injection, key-leak, prompt-leak, store and allergy overrides, oversized input, forced tool loop, tool-call flood, session cap, rate limit, an invented number and product, and the kung pao peanut case. I re-ran the demo after the diet fix (19/19 again); it has no diet case, and the diet check is covered by tests and logs/diet_fix_check.md.

Two live allergen runs

Peanut allergy, Kung pao chicken, Walmart. The first check flagged peanuts as a definite conflict and the substitution step was re-run once. Peanuts were left out of the recipe and struck through on the page; three other ingredients with no store match (dried red chilies, Chinese black vinegar and Shaoxing wine) were left out too, so four items were left out in total. The page shows a yellow warning, not a green box, because soy sauce, cornstarch and vegetable oil could not be confirmed peanut-free from the catalog or keyword list.

Fish allergy, Vietnamese chicken pho, Aldi (a fresh-clone check I ran; the run output was not saved in the repo): 44 seconds, 16,373 input tokens (4,328 cached, 5,406 cache-write), 3,794 output tokens, 11 requests, about $0.0033. The first pass flagged fish sauce and the substitution re-run removed it.

A problem the measurement found, and the fix

In the 20-run measurement, a gluten-allergy dish (Japanese chicken katsu curry) kept panko in the final recipe in both configurations, because the allergen keyword list had no entry for panko; it was only marked uncertain. I extended the keyword list (whole-word matching, so nutmeg and eggplant are not flagged). A before-and-after check on all saved results (logs/allergen_fix_check.md) shows only that dish changed (2 of 14 saved results with an allergy). A new live run flagged panko, flour and soy sauce, re-ran the substitution step, and removed all three. A later noodle check (with tests) found that rice vermicelli had been treated as safe for gluten rather than uncertain; rice, glass and sweet-potato noodles are now uncertain, and wheat noodles, ramen, udon and soba stay definite conflicts.

A second problem, found by a head-to-head comparison with a general chatbot

In the head-to-head test (section 3), HomeBite kept 120 g of pork belly in a vegetarian answer, because the dietary preference reached the AI only as text and no code checked it. I fixed it in the same style as the allergen path (see the risk table), and the steps are now also checked so they cannot use a left-out ingredient. Re-checked live with the original settings: pork belly was flagged on the first pass and removed through the re-run, and it is absent from the list and steps (logs/diet_fix_check.md); the page shows a yellow Diet check box for kimchi. Offline, the check flagged nothing on the 2 saved vegetarian ratatouille runs, and 18 of 18 saved results without a diet preference are unaffected. Halal and kosher are still only passed to the AI.

What is not proven

  • The role-play jailbreak case in the demo was stopped by the AI provider's own content filter before my classifier answered, so it does not show my classifier working.
  • The red not-safe screens for a remaining allergen or diet conflict were tested offline with a fake model only; in the live runs, the re-run always removed the conflict, and allergen behavior was observed on 7 dishes (14 runs) plus the live runs, never with a real catalog.
  • The diet check was verified live on one dish and offline on the saved results; it is a keyword list, not a guarantee, and the safety demo has no diet case.
  • The allergen check uses catalog tags and a keyword list. It is not a guarantee. Ingredients such as Worcestershire sauce stay uncertain, and the page asks the student to check the label.

7. Impact

Measured results are marked as measured; everything else is potential.

(a) One real user test

A friend, Alex, tried HomeBite in person on my laptop and agreed to be named by first name. He entered his mom's potato beef stew with Whole Foods selected, no allergies, the lower-sodium goal and 2 servings. The run took 18 seconds, used 5,458 input tokens (0 cached) and 1,776 output tokens over 5 requests, and cost an estimated $0.0015. No substitutions were needed (0 substitutes, 0 items left out). This was a single tester and a dish with no substitutions, so it tested usability, not the substitution engine.

He thought it was a cool concept, found the instructions easy to follow and the ingredient list clear. In his words: “This is so interesting! I can't wait to try recreating my mom's dishes with this!” His three ideas: allow multiple selections for allergens, dietary preferences and goals (for example low sodium and low calorie together; the allergy box already allows several choices, so he may not have noticed); show pictures of the dishes; and turn the input into a chatbot that talks with you about the dish. Two of those, pictures and conversation, are things ChatGPT did in the head-to-head test in section 3.

(b) Time and cost

My manual web search for one vegetarian kimchi jjigae recipe took about 2 minutes and gave a recipe only. HomeBite's measured run times were 16.1 to 56.6 seconds across the 20 runs (33.2 seconds on average for the baseline), and it returns an adapted list, steps, substitutes and a nutrition comparison. These are not like-for-like: one self-timed search for one dish against 20 runs of an app, and the search time excludes looking up nutrition. Cost, measured: $0.002414 per run on average ($0.003646 at p90); projected at 12 runs per user per month (my assumption): $0.03 per user per month.

(c) Quality measures

The cost-saver table in section 5 holds the catalog-valid, allergen-detection and residual-conflict rates. Not shown there: in the 10 baseline runs, 7 ingredients got a substitute and 18 were left out; 7 of 7 proposed baseline substitutes were found in the store catalog; the Writer needed a retry in 1 baseline run and fell back to the template in 0; 5 of 5 dishes with an expected allergen conflict were detected by the first check (I chose the expected words myself, and this was measured before the panko keyword fix); and 0 of 7 baseline runs with an allergy kept a conflict in the final recipe (the panko case was only marked uncertain then).

Measured: token use, cost and latency of 20 runs; safety demo results; one user test. Potential, not measured: time saved for students, savings in money, adoption, and any health benefit. For context only, not a forecast: 1,177,766 international students were enrolled at U.S. institutions in 2024/25; I have no data on how many would use an app like this.

8. Limits and next steps

What does not work yet

  • The catalog is a starter set of 163 illustrative items, none verified against real listings. Over the 10 baseline runs, only 7 ingredients got a substitute (table below).
  • The Goal selector (for example lower sodium) is passed to the AI as context but is not enforced or verified by code, and the results page does not say whether the goal was met. Allergies, the store and the vegetarian, vegan and pescatarian preferences are enforced by code; goals and other preferences (halal, kosher) are not.
  • Some ingredients have no USDA entry and are excluded from the nutrition totals (the page says which), so nutrition differences between the original and the adapted dish mostly reflect ingredients that were left out or have no USDA entry, not a healthier recipe. In a live kung pao run, calories fell by 82.66 and sodium rose by 161.59 mg, which is consistent with the original dish's dark soy sauce having no USDA entry (so it is excluded) while its substitute does.
  • When a check removes the main protein, HomeBite does not rebalance the dish: in the diet-fix example calories fell from 530.42 to 131.2 per serving, because the pork belly was removed and nothing replaced it, so the adapted dish is a very light stew, not a healthier recipe.
  • The starter catalog has no vegan-labeled kimchi, so HomeBite keeps generic kimchi with a check-the-label warning, where ChatGPT named a specific vegan-labeled product.
  • There are no dish pictures and no chat. The combined cost-saver did not raise caching. Most of the roughly 33 seconds is model generation, and I did not break latency down by stage.
  • Allergen checks are not a guarantee, and this is not medical advice. The Windows setup steps in the README are untested. Only one person tested the app.

What was left out, from the saved baseline runs

Over the 10 baseline runs, 7 ingredients got a substitute and 18 were left out (the same counts as section 7). The table lists every left-out ingredient from logs/measurement/results/; 3 of the 10 dishes had none. By store: Asian grocery 8, Walmart 5, Trader Joe's 3, Whole Foods 1, Aldi 1. In every case the saved result says no suitable product was found in that store's catalog; the stated reasons are in the saved results, and for five items (flour, egg, yogurt, butter, dried shrimp) they also mention an allergy or an ingredient conflict.

Three dishes had no ingredient left out, and the two Asian-grocery dishes account for 8 of the 18. That is a count from 10 dishes, so it shows where this starter catalog was thin, not why.

If I had another month

  • Use real, licensed store data and verify it, replacing the starter catalog. First add and verify the items in the table above (the sauces, pastes, spices and preserved items for the Asian-grocery and Walmart dishes), then re-run the same 10 dishes to see how many are still left out.
  • Have the Verifier compute whether a goal was met and show it on the page, and rebalance a dish when a check removes its main protein.
  • Allow several goals and diets at once.
  • Add conversational follow-ups, which would raise both cost and the safety surface.
  • Add dish images, after checking licensing.
  • Run a wider user study, with people who need substitutions.
  • Test the batched-lookup lever on its own, to find which lever lowered the nutrition match rate.
  • Add gluten-free and other allergen-safe items to the catalog, so the re-run has safe options to choose from.

  • Safety demo pass count and guard tokens; allergen fix (2 of 14 changed); diet check runs: logs/safety_demo_output.txt, logs/allergen_fix_check.md, logs/diet_fix_check.md.
  • Limits, caps and prices per million tokens: safety.py; usage.py (course slides, Cached Token Cost slide, gpt-6-luna row).
  • 268 tests; 3,000 USDA foods; 163 catalog items, 0 verified; repository URL: python -m pytest -q at build time (no tokens); data/*.csv; README.md; git remote.
  • Left-out ingredient table: logs/measurement/results/*_baseline.json (saved results, read by the build script).
  • Kung pao run totals, ChatGPT test and HomeBite test runs: usage screenshot and trace panels (section 4); the ChatGPT and HomeBite screenshots (section 3).
  • Author's own measurements and assumptions: Alex's test (18 s, 5,458 / 0 / 1,776 tokens, 5 requests, $0.0015; checked against his usage screenshot); manual search about 2 minutes; 12 runs per user per month; the Vietnamese chicken pho run and about 35 seconds from clone to a running page (a fresh-clone check I ran; output not saved in the repo); the two ChatGPT links I clicked.
